desc: The Gond are one of the largest tribal groups in India, with a population exceeding 13 million. They are concentrated in the Gondwana region of central India, spanning Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra, and Telangana. The Gond have a rich cultural heritage including Pardhan Gond paintings, traditional music, and the Gondi language. Historically, they ruled the Gondwana kingdom with centers at Garha-Mandla and Chanda. Their society is organized into clans and they practice both Hinduism and their own animistic traditions centered around nature worship.
fact: They are one of the largest tribal groups in India with over 13 million people · They are concentrated in the Gondwana region of central India · They have a rich tradition of Pardhan Gond painting, recognized globally · Historically they ruled the Gondwana kingdom with Garha-Mandla as capital

desc: The Bhil are one of the largest tribal communities in India, primarily distributed across Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, and Maharashtra. The name 'Bhil' is derived from the Dravidian word for 'bow,' reflecting their traditional skill as archers. Their population exceeds 17 million, making them the third-largest tribal group in India. The Bhil have a distinct culture including traditional Pithora paintings, the Ghoomar dance, and the Bhili language. They practice agriculture and forest-based livelihoods.
fact: The name 'Bhil' is derived from the Dravidian word for 'bow,' reflecting their archery tradition · They are among the largest tribal communities with over 17 million people · Their traditional Pithora wall paintings are a distinctive art form · The Ghoomar dance originated from the Bhil community

desc: The Santhal are one of the largest and most prominent tribal communities in eastern India, primarily inhabiting Jharkhand, West Bengal, Odisha, and Bihar. They are the largest tribal group in Jharkhand and speak Santali, an Austroasiatic language. The Santhal lead a distinctive uprising against British colonial rule in 1855, known as the Santhal Hool, led by Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu. They are known for their traditional music, Sohrai paintings, and vibrant festivals. Their society is egalitarian and they practice settled agriculture.
fact: They led the Santhal Hool in 1855, a major uprising against British colonial rule · They are the largest tribal group in Jharkhand · They speak Santali, an Austroasiatic language · Sohrai paintings are a distinctive Santhal art tradition celebrated during harvest festivals

desc: The Munda are a major Austroasiatic tribal group predominantly found in the Chhota Nagpur Plateau region of Jharkhand. They speak Mundari, an Austroasiatic language. The Munda were the focal point of the Birsa Munda-led rebellion against British rule in 1899-1900, and their leader Birsa Munda is revered as a tribal icon across India. They are traditionally agrarian, practicing both settled and shifting agriculture. Munda society is clan-based with a deep connection to forests and nature, and they follow the Sarna religion.
fact: Birsa Munda, the legendary tribal leader who rebelled against British rule, belonged to the Munda community · They are predominantly found in the Chhota Nagpur Plateau of Jharkhand · They speak Mundari, an Austroasiatic language · They follow the Sarna religion with worship of nature and ancestral spirits

desc: The Khasi are one of the major tribal communities of Meghalaya, inhabiting the Khasi Hills and Jaintia Hills districts. They speak the Khasi language, an Austroasiatic language, and are known for practicing a matrilineal society where lineage and inheritance pass through the mother. The Khasi are known for their unique living root bridges, woven from the roots of rubber fig trees over generations. They have a distinct culture with traditional festivals like Nongkrem and Shad Suk Mynsiem. The community has a high literacy rate and is predominantly Christian with some traditional Khasism followers.
fact: The Khasi practice one of the world's few surviving matrilineal systems · They are known for unique living root bridges grown from rubber fig tree roots · They speak Khasi, an Austroasiatic language · The Nongkrem dance festival is a major Khasi cultural celebration

desc: The Naga is a collective term for several indigenous communities inhabiting Nagaland and neighboring states in Northeast India. There are 16 officially recognized Naga tribes including the Angami, Ao, Sema, Lotha, and Konyak. Each tribe has its own distinct language, traditional attire, and customs. The Naga are known for their rich warrior tradition, colorful hornbill festivals, and intricate beadwork and shawl weaving. Traditionally, they practiced headhunting, which was abandoned with the arrival of Christianity in the 19th and 20th centuries. The Hornbill Festival is a showcase of Naga culture held annually in Kohima.
fact: The Naga collectively refers to 16 officially recognized tribes including Angami, Ao, and Konyak · The annual Hornbill Festival is a celebrated showcase of Naga culture · They are known for their warrior tradition, intricate beadwork, and shawl weaving · Headhunting was traditionally practiced but abandoned with the arrival of Christianity

desc: The Bodo are one of the largest tribal communities in Assam, primarily concentrated in the Bodoland Territorial Region along the northern bank of the Brahmaputra River. They speak the Bodo language, a Tibeto-Burman language. The Bodo are known for their traditional rice cultivation, bamboo craft, and weaving skills. Their traditional dress reflects intricate handloom patterns, especially the Dokhona worn by women. The Bodo celebrate the Kwathri and Magh Bwisagu festivals with music and dance. They have a strong cultural identity and the Bodo language has official status in Assam.
fact: The Bodo are concentrated in the Bodoland region of Assam along the Brahmaputra · They speak Bodo, a Tibeto-Burman language with official status in Assam · They are known for traditional rice cultivation, bamboo craft, and handloom weaving · The Kwathri and Magh Bwisagu are major Bodo festivals

desc: The Mizo are a Tibeto-Burman ethnic group native to Mizoram, with related communities in Manipur, Assam, and Tripura. The term 'Mizo' encompasses several sub-tribes including the Lushai, Hmar, Ralte, and Paite. Mizo society is known for its high literacy rate, among the highest in India. Traditionally, they practiced jhum (slash-and-burn) cultivation and lived in distinctive bamboo houses built on hilltops. The Mizo have a rich tradition of folk songs, dances like Cheraw (bamboo dance), and festivals. Christianity became dominant in the 20th century. The Mizo Hills were the site of a major famine in 1959-60 that led to the formation of Mizoram state.
fact: The Mizo have one of the highest literacy rates in India · Cheraw, the bamboo dance, is the most famous Mizo folk dance · The great Mizo famine of 1959-60 led to political reorganization and statehood · They traditionally practiced jhum cultivation in bamboo houses on hilltops

desc: The Tharu are a tribal community living in the Terai plains of the Himalayan foothills, spanning Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Bihar, and neighboring Nepal. They are known for their remarkable genetic immunity to malaria, which allowed them to inhabit the dense, mosquito-infested Terai forests that outsiders avoided. The Tharu live in distinctive longhouses made of bamboo and mud, with elaborate painted murals on walls. They practice agriculture, fishing, and forest gathering. Their women wear distinctive silver jewelry and traditional tattoo markings. The Tharu speak various Indo-Aryan dialects with Tibeto-Burman influences.
fact: The Tharu have remarkable genetic immunity to malaria, enabling them to inhabit the Terai forests · They live in distinctive decorated longhouses made of bamboo and mud · Their women are known for elaborate silver jewelry and traditional tattoos · They are spread across the Himalayan Terai from Uttarakhand to Bihar and Nepal

desc: The Toda are a pastoral tribal community living in the Nilgiri Hills of Tamil Nadu. They are one of the most distinctive tribal groups in India, with a population of about 2,000 people. The Toda are traditionally buffalo herders, and their dairy culture is central to their society and religion. They live in unique barrel-vaulted huts called 'dogles' made of bamboo and thatch. The Toda are known for their distinctive black-and-red embroidered shawls. Their language, Toda, belongs to the Dravidian family. The Toda have preserved their unique traditions while living in close proximity to modern settlements in the Nilgiris.
fact: The Toda are traditional buffalo herders in the Nilgiri Hills · They live in unique barrel-vaulted huts called dogles · They are known for distinctive black-and-red embroidered shawls · Their dairy culture and buffalo-centric religion are central to Toda society

desc: The Warli are an indigenous tribal community living in the Palghar district of Maharashtra, north of Mumbai. They are world-famous for their distinctive Warli painting tradition, one of the oldest art forms in India, dating back to 2500 BCE. Warli paintings use geometric patterns of circles, triangles, and squares to depict daily life, hunting, farming, and festivals. The paintings are traditionally done on mud walls using white pigment made from rice flour. The community speaks the Warli language, an Indo-Aryan dialect. Their main festival is celebrating the harvest season and they practice both agriculture and forest-based livelihoods.
fact: Warli painting is one of the oldest art forms in India, dating to 2500 BCE · Paintings use geometric patterns in white pigment on mud walls · The Warli community lives primarily in Palghar district, Maharashtra · The paintings depict daily life, hunting, farming, and festivals

desc: The Apatani are a tribal community inhabiting the Ziro Valley in the Lower Subansiri district of Arunachal Pradesh. They are known for their advanced wet rice cultivation system integrated with fish farming, a remarkable example of sustainable indigenous agriculture. The Apatani are also noted for their traditional practice of facial tattoos and nose plugs, which is now largely discontinued. Their Ziro Valley is a UNESCO World Heritage Site candidate. Apatani society is democratic and they practice the Donyi-Polo (Sun-Moon) religion alongside Christianity. Their annual Myoko festival celebrates friendship and peace among villages.
fact: The Apatani practice an advanced wet rice cultivation system integrated with fish farming in Ziro Valley · Their Ziro Valley is a UNESCO World Heritage Site candidate · Traditional facial tattoos and nose plugs are a distinctive (now discontinued) Apatani practice · The Myoko festival celebrates inter-village friendship and peace

desc: The Siddi are an Afro-Indian tribal community primarily living in the Uttara Kannada and Yellapur regions of Karnataka, with smaller populations in Gujarat, Maharashtra, and Goa. They are descendants of Bantu East African people who were brought to India as slaves, merchants, sailors, and soldiers by Arab, Portuguese, and British traders between the 7th and 19th centuries. The Siddi have preserved their African heritage through music and dance, particularly the Siddi Dhamal and Goma traditions. They speak a dialect of Kannada and Konkani. Their population is around 60,000 in India and they are recognized as a Scheduled Tribe.
fact: The Siddi are descendants of East African Bantu people brought to India over centuries · They live primarily in Uttara Kannada district of Karnataka · They preserved African heritage through Siddi Dhamal and Goma music and dance · Their population is about 60,000, recognized as a Scheduled Tribe

desc: The Jarawa are one of the indigenous Andamanese tribes living in the Andaman Islands. They inhabit the western coast of South and Middle Andaman Islands. The Jarawa have maintained their traditional hunter-gatherer lifestyle and have had limited contact with the outside world. Their population is estimated at around 400 individuals. The Andaman Trunk Road, which passes through their reserve, has led to increased contact and potential health risks. The Jarawa speak the Jarawan language, part of the Andamanese language family, and are protected under Indian law with strict regulations on contact and photography.
fact: The Jarawa are one of the indigenous hunter-gatherer tribes of the Andaman Islands · Their population is estimated at around 400 individuals · They inhabit western South and Middle Andaman Islands · The Andaman Trunk Road through their territory has increased contact risks

desc: The Sentinelese are an indigenous people living on North Sentinel Island in the Andaman Islands. They are one of the last uncontacted peoples in the world, maintaining complete isolation from modern civilization. Their population is estimated between 50 and 200 individuals. The Sentinelese are hunter-gatherers who use bows, arrows, and spears for hunting and self-defense. They have consistently resisted all external contact, famously attacking outsiders who approach their island. The Indian government enforces a strict no-contact policy, prohibiting approach within 5 nautical miles of the island to protect the tribe from diseases and cultural disruption.
fact: The Sentinelese are one of the last uncontacted peoples in the world · They maintain complete isolation on North Sentinel Island · They have consistently resisted all external contact for centuries · The Indian government enforces a strict no-contact policy within 5 nautical miles

desc: The Rabari are a pastoral tribal community primarily found in the Kutch and Saurashtra regions of Gujarat, with populations in Rajasthan and Punjab. Traditionally, they are camel, cattle, goat, and sheep herders who follow a nomadic or semi-nomadic lifestyle. The Rabari are known for their distinctive embroidered textiles, mirror-work, and intricate jewelry. Rabari women wear black skirts and embroidered blouses with heavy silver ornaments. Their men traditionally wear white with a distinctive turban. The Rabari have a strong oral tradition and worship the goddess Mata and the folk deity Ramdev Pir. The community is recognized as a Scheduled Tribe in Gujarat.
fact: The Rabari are traditional pastoralists herding camels, cattle, goats, and sheep in Gujarat · They are known for distinctive embroidered textiles with intricate mirror-work · Rabari women wear black skirts with heavy silver jewelry · The community is primarily found in Kutch and Saurashtra regions of Gujarat
